screens.title: Classes, Objects, and Structs in Unreal Engine C++
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a clear mental model for how classes, objects, and structs work inside Unreal Engine. You'll learn what makes an ordinary C++ type different from an engine-aware type, why macros like UCLASS and USTRUCT matter, and how GENERATED_BODY, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION let your code appear in the editor and be safe under Unreal's memory model. We will ground these ideas with concrete examples: creating a simple actor with an editable property and a Blueprint-callable function, and declaring a lightweight data struct that can be used in Blueprints. Along the way I will point out common mistakes that cause compile errors or invisible properties in the editor, and show how to avoid dangling pointers by using UE smart pointer types. By the end you will understand the reflection system's role, when to inherit from AActor or UObject, and how to decide between a USTRUCT and a UCLASS for your data. Think about a game object you want to expose to designers — this chapter shows the exact steps to make that happen safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to name, explain, and use engine-aware types in Unreal C++. First, you'll explain classes as blueprints and objects as instances, and show a concrete example such as a collectible actor with editable properties. Second, you'll distinguish plain C++ classes and structs from UCLASS and USTRUCT variants, describing why macros are required for reflection and editor integration. Third, you'll declare and define a custom actor class that compiles and appears in the editor, including how to add a UPROPERTY and a UFUNCTION. Fourth, you'll reason about memory: explain Unreal's garbage collection and when to use weak or soft pointers to avoid dangling references. Each objective is tied to a verified competency milestone so you can check that your class appears in the editor, the property is editable, and the function can be called from Blueprints. These are practical, testable skills that make your C++ code usable by designers and safe at runtime.

screens.title: Classes and Objects: Blueprints and Instances
screens.narratorSegment: A class is a blueprint: it defines the data and behavior an entity can have, such as properties for speed or health and functions for actions. An object — also called an instance — is a concrete realization of that blueprint with its own values. For example, you might declare a FighterJet class that defines MaxSpeed and FireWeapon; each plane placed in a level is an object with its own MaxSpeed setting and current fuel. In Unreal C++ you still use standard C++ classes for logic, but when you want editor integration you annotate types with engine macros. One common misconception is thinking that declaring a class automatically makes it available in the editor; it does not. Without UCLASS, Unreal's reflection tools cannot see your types, they cannot show properties in the Details panel, and Blueprints cannot reference them. Another common mistake is confusing 'struct' and 'class' based on C++ syntax alone; in Unreal the usage differs by intent: structs are lightweight data containers, while classes that inherit from UObject or AActor participate in the engine's object model and lifecycle. Practical example: design a Collectible class with a CollectibleValue property. When you instantiate that class as an actor in the level you now have an object designers can place and customize. Takeaway: know whether you need editor integration, serialization, or GC — that determines whether your type should be an ordinary C++ class, a USTRUCT, or a UCLASS-derived type.

keyIdea.text: Class: blueprint. Object: instance with unique state. In Unreal, choose UCLASS/USTRUCT when you need engine features.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Classes & Objects
Class as Blueprint
A class groups member variables and functions into a single unit. It does not consume game memory until instantiated.
Concrete example
A FighterJet class defines MaxSpeed and FireWeapon. An F-16 object is an instance with real MaxSpeed and state.
Common misconception
Declaring a C++ class does not automatically expose it to the Unreal Editor. You must use UCLASS and GENERATED_BODY for reflection.
Why it matters
Choosing the wrong kind of type can block editor access, Blueprint calls, or proper memory handling at runtime.
Object as Instance
An object holds runtime state and reacts to engine events, such as BeginPlay or Tick if it inherits AActor.
Analogy
Think of a class as a cookie cutter and objects as the cookies. Each cookie can be decorated differently while using the same cutter.
Check your understanding
  • Do you need editor placement or Blueprint access?
  • If yes, consider inheriting from AActor or using USTRUCT/UCLASS.
Key Takeaway

Only engine-aware types annotated for reflection become visible and manageable inside Unreal Editor and Blueprints.

screens.title: UCLASS() and USTRUCT(): What They Do
screens.narratorSegment: UCLASS and USTRUCT are macros that mark your C++ types for Unreal's reflection system. They do more than add metadata: they instruct the Unreal Header Tool to generate code that registers properties, functions, and type information so the editor, Blueprints, serialization, and networking systems can work with your type. In practice, marking a class with UCLASS and placing GENERATED_BODY inside the class body causes the build pipeline to produce boilerplate code that wires your class to the engine. Without these macros, your C++ type remains invisible to these systems. A concrete example: add UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) to an int32 field and it will appear in the Details panel where designers can change it. A common misconception is that these macros are optional or merely stylistic; they are required whenever you expect editor integration, Blueprint access, or garbage collection. Another important nuance is the difference in intent: use USTRUCT for small data containers you want to expose and serialize, and UCLASS when you need a UObject-derived type with engine lifecycle features. Closing question: which of your data types will need runtime features like BeginPlay or replication, and therefore should be a UCLASS rather than a USTRUCT?

keyIdea.title: Macro purpose
keyIdea.text: UCLASS/USTRUCT enable the Unreal Header Tool to generate the reflection glue that makes C++ types visible to engine systems.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › UCLASS & USTRUCT
What the macros do
They trigger code generation and register metadata so the engine can inspect and use your types.
Reflection & Editor
Properties annotated with UPROPERTY become visible in the Details panel and editable by designers.
Blueprint access
UFUNCTION and UPROPERTY specifiers control whether Blueprints can call functions or read/write fields.
Concrete example
Mark an int32 with UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite); it will appear in the Details panel when the actor is selected.
Quick contrast
Plain C++ types: compile and run, but invisible to the editor. UHT types: visible, serializable, and integrated with GC and Blueprint systems.
Misconception

These macros are not just comments: omitting them prevents the engine from generating the required glue code and often causes compile-time or editor failures.

screens.title: What GENERATED_BODY() Actually Provides
screens.narratorSegment: GENERATED_BODY is the macro you place inside a UCLASS or USTRUCT declaration; it expands into the boilerplate that registers the type, its properties, and its functions with the engine. Think of GENERATED_BODY as the bridge between your readable header and the engine's hidden registration system. The build tool runs the Unreal Header Tool, which scans headers for UCLASS/USTRUCT annotations and produces generated code that is then compiled along with your project. In practice, forgetting GENERATED_BODY commonly produces cryptic compile errors because the registration functions are missing. A concrete sequence: write the header with UCLASS and GENERATED_BODY, run the build which triggers UHT, compiled generated code registers UUObject constructors and property metadata, then the editor can show fields and Blueprints can call functions. A common misconception is that GENERATED_BODY is optional or replaceable by manual code; the UHT output contains specific metadata and function signatures that are not practical to hand-write. Takeaway: always include GENERATED_BODY in UCLASS/USTRUCT definitions; it is the single point that enables reflection, serialization, and many editor features. What GENERATED_BODY() Actually Provides means generated_body expands to registration and metadata code created by the unreal header tool; it is mandatory for reflected types.. In practical terms, understand the essential boilerplate wire-up for uht. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › GENERATED_BODY
Build-time process
How UHT and GENERATED_BODY connect your header to the engine.
1. Annotate
Add UCLASS/USTRUCT and GENERATED_BODY to headers.
2. UHT runs
The Unreal Header Tool scans and generates glue code with metadata tables.
3. Compile
Generated code compiles with your project to provide registration functions.
4. Editor integration
Properties and functions are now visible in Details and Blueprints.
Concrete symptom
Missing GENERATED_BODY often yields linker or registration errors because expected symbols are not present.
Checklist
  • UCLASS/USTRUCT present
  • GENERATED_BODY included inside class/struct
  • Header included in module build

screens.title: Declaring an Actor: AMyCollectible Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a clean header declaration for a collectible actor so you see the required pieces in context. The header uses UCLASS to mark the type, then GENERATED_BODY inside the class body to give the engine its registration code. Public sections declare constructors and engine callbacks like BeginPlay, and members annotated with UPROPERTY control editor and Blueprint visibility. For example, adding UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Collectible") before an int32 CollectibleValue makes that field editable in the Details panel and accessible to Blueprints. We also declare a UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable) so the function can be triggered from Blueprints or tested at runtime. A common mistake is forgetting to include the generated header include line, which is required for UHT to find and process the macros. Practically, after saving this header you compile, then place the actor in a level and adjust the CollectibleValue in the Details panel to verify exposure. This step directly links the code you write to the editor experience designers use every day. In practical terms, header declaration with uclass, generated_body, uproperty and ufunction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › AMyCollectible Header
Header example
This code is a practical declaration you can compile and test in the editor.
// MyCollectible.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Actor.h"
#include "MyCollectible.generated.h" // Required for UCLASS()

UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AMyCollectible : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY() // Required for UCLASS()

public:
    AMyCollectible();

protected:
    virtual void BeginPlay() override;

public:
    virtual void Tick(float DeltaTime) override;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Collectible")
    int32 CollectibleValue;

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Collectible")
    void OnCollected();
};
Explanation
  • Include the generated header so UHT can process macros.
  • GENERATED_BODY expands to engine registration code.
  • UPROPERTY controls editor visibility and Blueprint access.
  • UFUNCTION makes methods callable by Blueprints when marked BlueprintCallable.
Key Takeaway

This header is the minimal, testable contract for an actor visible and editable in the Unreal Editor.

screens.title: Implementing Actor Methods and Testing in Runtime
screens.narratorSegment: Implementation connects your header declarations to runtime behavior. In the MySimpleActor example the constructor sets default values and configures ticking, BeginPlay runs once when the actor is spawned, and Tick runs every frame when enabled. A good test is to call your BlueprintCallable function in BeginPlay or from the editor: use engine logging and on-screen messages to verify that the function runs and that the property values propagate. For example, setting MyFloatValue = 100.0f in the constructor provides a visible default. In BeginPlay you can call PrintMyValue which uses the engine's logging and on-screen debug message to show the value. A common pitfall is modifying UPROPERTY values only in the constructor and expecting the editor-set values to persist after compile; remember the editor can override defaults when an instance is already placed, so test by placing a fresh actor in the level after compiling. Finally, ensure you include Engine headers used by logging calls and that you guard code paths when GEngine may be null in some contexts. The practical test loop: compile, place actor, edit property, run, and observe log and on-screen output to confirm behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Implementation
MySimpleActor.cpp (selected excerpts)
Use logging and on-screen messages to confirm behavior at runtime.
// MySimpleActor.cpp
#include "MySimpleActor.h"
#include "Engine/Engine.h" // For GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage

AMySimpleActor::AMySimpleActor()
{
    PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
    MyFloatValue = 100.0f; // Default value
}

void AMySimpleActor::BeginPlay()
{
    Super::BeginPlay();
    PrintMyValue(); // Test call
}

void AMySimpleActor::Tick(float DeltaTime)
{
    Super::Tick(DeltaTime);
}

void AMySimpleActor::PrintMyValue()
{
    if (GEngine)
    {
        GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Green, FString::Printf(TEXT("MyFloatValue is: %f"), MyFloatValue));
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("MyFloatValue is: %f"), MyFloatValue);
    }
}
Guidance & Common pitfall
If an actor was placed before you changed default values, the placed instance may keep the old defaults. Re-place the actor to see constructor defaults. If logging doesn't appear, ensure GEngine is valid and you have the correct log category.
Key Takeaway

Use on-screen debug messages and logs to verify that UFUNCTIONs run and UPROPERTY values were set as expected at runtime.

screens.title: Declaring and Using USTRUCT: FMyCustomData
screens.narratorSegment: USTRUCT is ideal for grouping related data that you want to serialize or expose as a single variable in Blueprints. A typical pattern is USTRUCT(BlueprintType) with GENERATED_BODY followed by UPROPERTY fields for each member. For example, an FMyCustomData struct with ID, Name, and Value fields lets designers edit grouped data in the Details panel and pass the struct through Blueprints. One concrete advantage over a plain C++ struct is that USTRUCT participates in the reflection system, so property editors, replication, and serialization can operate on it automatically. A common misconception is thinking that large, behavior-rich types should be USTRUCTS; if you need lifecycle methods, GC, or inheritance from UObject, use UCLASS instead. Also, include a default constructor to ensure members are initialized predictably. Practical workflow: declare your USTRUCT, compile, then create a UPROPERTY of that struct type on a UCLASS so the editor shows the nested fields. That verifies your struct is correctly exposed and serialized when you save levels or assets. In practical terms, lightweight data containers exposed to blueprints and serialization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Also, include a default constructor to ensure members are initialized predictably. Practical workflow: declare your USTRUCT, compile, then create a UPROPERTY of that struct type on a UCLASS so the editor shows the nested fields. That verifies your struct is correctly exposed and serialized when you save levels or assets. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › USTRUCT Example
FMyCustomData
A struct declaration you can use as a variable type in Blueprints.
// MyStruct.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "MyStruct.generated.h" // Required for USTRUCT()

USTRUCT(BlueprintType) // BlueprintType allows it to be used in Blueprints
struct FMyCustomData
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Custom Data")
    int32 ID;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Custom Data")
    FString Name;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Custom Data")
    float Value;

    FMyCustomData()
        : ID(0)
        , Name(TEXT("Default"))
        , Value(0.0f)
    {}
};
Practical guidance
Use USTRUCT when you need an editable grouped value in the editor or Blueprint variable type. For behavior or lifecycle, prefer UObject-derived classes.

A USTRUCT gives you structured, editor-visible data without the overhead of UObject-based memory management.

screens.title: UPROPERTY & UFUNCTION: Exposed vs Private Members
screens.narratorSegment: UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers determine what parts of your class are visible to designers and Blueprints. UPROPERTY with EditAnywhere allows properties to be edited in the Details panel, while BlueprintReadWrite permits Blueprint scripts to read and write the value. UFUNCTION marked BlueprintCallable makes a method invokable from Blueprints. A useful mental model is to split members into three categories: editor-exposed (designer-facing), Blueprint-facing (scripting A P I), and private implementation details (internal logic). A common mistake is over-exposing implementation details by making everything public with UPROPERTY; that leads to tight coupling between designers and engine code. Another pitfall is forgetting the correct specifiers, producing a member that compiles but is invisible in the editor. Concretely, if your CollectibleValue must be editable by designers and adjustable by Blueprints, use UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite). If a helper variable should remain internal, omit UPROPERTY entirely or use private non-UPROPERTY fields. Final question: for each member you write, ask whether designers need to see it, Blueprints need to access it, or it should stay internal to C++ logic. Exposed Members
Editor and Blueprint specifiers you commonly use.
EditAnywhere
Makes a property editable in the Details panel for placed instances and defaults.

screens.title: Memory Management and Garbage Collection
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's garbage collector manages the lifetime of UObject-derived instances. That means you generally should not manually delete UObjects; the engine will destroy them when there are no strong references. A crucial implication: storing raw pointers to UObjects can lead to dangling references if the object is garbage collected. To avoid this, prefer UE pointer types designed for safety: TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning ephemeral references, and TSoftObjectPtr for references that can be loaded on demand or survive asset unloading. Another pattern is using UPROPERTY pointers; when a UObject pointer is declared with UPROPERTY, the garbage collector treats that reference as a root and prevents collection as long as the owning object exists. A common misconception is assuming raw C++ pointers behave the same as UObject pointers; they do not. For concrete advice, if a field points to another actor that may be destroyed during gameplay, wrap it in TWeakObjectPtr or mark the pointer as UPROPERTY if you intend to guarantee lifetime. When debugging lifecycle issues, log object creation and destruction events and consider using IsValid checks before dereferencing. Takeaway: choose the pointer type based on ownership and lifetime expectations to avoid crashes and leaks.

screens.title: Compilation Errors and Missing Editor Integration
screens.narratorSegment: When a class does not appear in the editor or properties are missing, the cause is often a build-time or macro issue. Common root causes include forgetting the generated include line, omitting GENERATED_BODY, or incorrect module export macros like MYPROJECT_API. Another frequent problem is not recompiling the module after header changes; the Unreal Header Tool must run to regenerate glue code. If you see linker errors referencing missing registration functions, check for missing GENERATED_BODY or malformed UCLASS declarations. For properties that don't show in Details, ensure the field is declared with UPROPERTY and has appropriate specifiers like EditAnywhere. For functions not callable in Blueprints, use UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable). A typical troubleshooting workflow: re-run a full build so UHT processes headers, check for compiler or UHT errors in the output, ensure the generated header exists alongside your header, and re-place the actor in the level after compile. Misinterpreting warnings as harmless is a mistake—UHT warnings often indicate metadata issues that will prevent editor features. Final takeaway: treat the build log and UHT messages as primary diagnostic sources to restore editor integration. screens.title: Design Decisions: When to Use USTRUCT, UCLASS, or Plain C++
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between plain C++ types, USTRUCT, and UCLASS is a key design decision. Use plain C++ classes or structs when you need lightweight helpers that do not require editor exposure or serialization. Use USTRUCT when you need to group data for editor editing, Blueprint variables, or serialization but do not need UObject features like garbage collection or lifecycle events. Use UCLASS (often inheriting from AActor or UObject) when you need engine-managed lifetimes, placement in the world, ticking, or replication. Another practical rule: prefer USTRUCT for value-like data passed by copy, and UCLASS for reference types managed by the engine. Keep UPROPERTY exposure minimal and intentional: expose what designers need and keep implementation details private. For pointers, prefer UPROPERTY for owned references, TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning runtime references, and TSoftObjectPtr for optional asset references that may be unloaded. Lastly, document each type's intended use next to its declaration: future maintainers will thank you, and the editor-visible structure will match your design intent. Closing question: what trade-offs will you accept between performance, serialization, and editor convenience for your next feature? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a clear mental model for how classes, objects, and structs work inside Unreal Engine. You'll learn what makes an ordinary C++ type different from an engine-aware type, why macros like UCLASS and USTRUCT matter, and how GENERATED_BODY, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION let your code appear in the editor and be safe under Unreal's memory model. We will ground these ideas with concrete examples: creating a simple actor with an editable property and a Blueprint-callable function, and declaring a lightweight data struct that can be used in Blueprints. Along the way I will point out common mistakes that cause compile errors or invisible properties in the editor, and show how to avoid dangling pointers by using UE smart pointer types. By the end you will understand the reflection system's role, when to inherit from AActor or UObject, and how to decide between a USTRUCT and a UCLASS for your data. Think about a game object you want to expose to designers — this chapter shows the exact steps to make that happen safely.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to name, explain, and use engine-aware types in Unreal C++. First, you'll explain classes as blueprints and objects as instances, and show a concrete example such as a collectible actor with editable properties. Second, you'll distinguish plain C++ classes and structs from UCLASS and USTRUCT variants, describing why macros are required for reflection and editor integration. Third, you'll declare and define a custom actor class that compiles and appears in the editor, including how to add a UPROPERTY and a UFUNCTION. Fourth, you'll reason about memory: explain Unreal's garbage collection and when to use weak or soft pointers to avoid dangling references. Each objective is tied to a verified competency milestone so you can check that your class appears in the editor, the property is editable, and the function can be called from Blueprints. These are practical, testable skills that make your C++ code usable by designers and safe at runtime.

This second objectives slide lists measurable skills you'll practice during the hands-on work. You will declare a UCLASS-derived actor that compiles and appears in the Content Browser, add a UPROPERTY that is editable in the Details panel, and write a UFUNCTION that Blueprints can call. You will also declare a USTRUCT with GENERATED_BODY so it can be used as a Blueprint variable type and serialized. Finally, you will exercise safe pointer patterns by explaining when to use TWeakObjectPtr or TSoftObjectPtr to reference objects that might be garbage collected. Each task maps to a verification step: compile without errors, drag the actor into a level, change the property in the Details panel, and observe log output when a function runs. These steps reinforce not just syntax but the practical integration points that make C++ useful inside Unreal Editor workflows.

A class is a blueprint: it defines the data and behavior an entity can have, such as properties for speed or health and functions for actions. An object — also called an instance — is a concrete realization of that blueprint with its own values. For example, you might declare a FighterJet class that defines MaxSpeed and FireWeapon; each plane placed in a level is an object with its own MaxSpeed setting and current fuel. In Unreal C++ you still use standard C++ classes for logic, but when you want editor integration you annotate types with engine macros. One common misconception is thinking that declaring a class automatically makes it available in the editor; it does not. Without UCLASS, Unreal's reflection tools cannot see your types, they cannot show properties in the Details panel, and Blueprints cannot reference them. Another common mistake is confusing 'struct' and 'class' based on C++ syntax alone; in Unreal the usage differs by intent: structs are lightweight data containers, while classes that inherit from UObject or AActor participate in the engine's object model and lifecycle. UCLASS and USTRUCT are macros that mark your C++ types for Unreal's reflection system. They do more than add metadata: they instruct the Unreal Header Tool to generate code that registers properties, functions, and type information so the editor, Blueprints, serialization, and networking systems can work with your type. In practice, marking a class with UCLASS and placing GENERATED_BODY inside the class body causes the build pipeline to produce boilerplate code that wires your class to the engine. Without these macros, your C++ type remains invisible to these systems. A concrete example: add UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) to an int32 field and it will appear in the Details panel where designers can change it. A common misconception is that these macros are optional or merely stylistic; they are required whenever you expect editor integration, Blueprint access, or garbage collection. Another important nuance is the difference in intent: use USTRUCT for small data containers you want to expose and serialize, and UCLASS when you need a UObject-derived type with engine lifecycle features. Closing question: which of your data types will need runtime features like BeginPlay or replication, and therefore should be a UCLASS rather than a USTRUCT?

GENERATED_BODY is the macro you place inside a UCLASS or USTRUCT declaration; it expands into the boilerplate that registers the type, its properties, and its functions with the engine. Think of GENERATED_BODY as the bridge between your readable header and the engine's hidden registration system. The build tool runs the Unreal Header Tool, which scans headers for UCLASS/USTRUCT annotations and produces generated code that is then compiled along with your project. In practice, forgetting GENERATED_BODY commonly produces cryptic compile errors because the registration functions are missing. A concrete sequence: write the header with UCLASS and GENERATED_BODY, run the build which triggers UHT, compiled generated code registers UUObject constructors and property metadata, then the editor can show fields and Blueprints can call functions. A common misconception is that GENERATED_BODY is optional or replaceable by manual code; the UHT output contains specific metadata and function signatures that are not practical to hand-write. Takeaway: always include GENERATED_BODY in UCLASS/USTRUCT definitions; it is the single point that enables reflection, serialization, and many editor features. One concrete advantage over a plain C++ struct is that USTRUCT participates in the reflection system, so property editors, replication, and serialization can operate on it automatically. A common misconception is thinking that large, behavior-rich types should be USTRUCTS; if you need lifecycle methods, GC, or inheritance from UObject, use UCLASS instead. UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers determine what parts of your class are visible to designers and Blueprints. UPROPERTY with EditAnywhere allows properties to be edited in the Details panel, while BlueprintReadWrite permits Blueprint scripts to read and write the value. UFUNCTION marked BlueprintCallable makes a method invokable from Blueprints. A useful mental model is to split members into three categories: editor-exposed (designer-facing), Blueprint-facing (scripting A P I), and private implementation details (internal logic). A common mistake is over-exposing implementation details by making everything public with UPROPERTY; that leads to tight coupling between designers and engine code. Another pitfall is forgetting the correct specifiers, producing a member that compiles but is invisible in the editor. Concretely, if your CollectibleValue must be editable by designers and adjustable by Blueprints, use UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite). Unreal's garbage collector manages the lifetime of UObject-derived instances. That means you generally should not manually delete UObjects; the engine will destroy them when there are no strong references. A crucial implication: storing raw pointers to UObjects can lead to dangling references if the object is garbage collected. To avoid this, prefer UE pointer types designed for safety: TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning ephemeral references, and TSoftObjectPtr for references that can be loaded on demand or survive asset unloading. Another pattern is using UPROPERTY pointers; when a UObject pointer is declared with UPROPERTY, the garbage collector treats that reference as a root and prevents collection as long as the owning object exists. A common misconception is assuming raw C++ pointers behave the same as UObject pointers; they do not. For concrete advice, if a field points to another actor that may be destroyed during gameplay, wrap it in TWeakObjectPtr or mark the pointer as UPROPERTY if you intend to guarantee lifetime. When debugging lifecycle issues, log object creation and destruction events and consider using IsValid checks before dereferencing. Takeaway: choose the pointer type based on ownership and lifetime expectations to avoid crashes and leaks.

Another frequent problem is not recompiling the module after header changes; the Unreal Header Tool must run to regenerate glue code. If you see linker errors referencing missing registration functions, check for missing GENERATED_BODY or malformed UCLASS declarations. For properties that don't show in Details, ensure the field is declared with UPROPERTY and has appropriate specifiers like EditAnywhere. For functions not callable in Blueprints, use UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable). A typical troubleshooting workflow: re-run a full build so UHT processes headers, check for compiler or UHT errors in the output, ensure the generated header exists alongside your header, and re-place the actor in the level after compile. Misinterpreting warnings as harmless is a mistake—UHT warnings often indicate metadata issues that will prevent editor features. Choosing between plain C++ types, USTRUCT, and UCLASS is a key design decision. Use plain C++ classes or structs when you need lightweight helpers that do not require editor exposure or serialization. Use USTRUCT when you need to group data for editor editing, Blueprint variables, or serialization but do not need UObject features like garbage collection or lifecycle events. Use UCLASS (often inheriting from AActor or UObject) when you need engine-managed lifetimes, placement in the world, ticking, or replication. Another practical rule: prefer USTRUCT for value-like data passed by copy, and UCLASS for reference types managed by the engine. Keep UPROPERTY exposure minimal and intentional: expose what designers need and keep implementation details private. For pointers, prefer UPROPERTY for owned references, TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning runtime references, and TSoftObjectPtr for optional asset references that may be unloaded. Lastly, document each type's intended use next to its declaration: future maintainers will thank you, and the editor-visible structure will match your design intent. Second, UCLASS, USTRUCT, and GENERATED_BODY are not optional decorations — they register your types with Unreal's reflection system so the editor, Blueprints, and serialization work.
